title: Lesson 2: Basic Computer Hardware
subtitle: Build a real computer from scratch, piece by piece, and watch it power up.

learningFocus.summary: In this Primary 2 Computer Skills activity, students open up a computer case and build a working machine from its five main components, practising the digital-literacy skill of recognising real hardware and matching each part to its job. Deciding where every part belongs before it snaps into place builds sequencing and critical-thinking skills, while the Explain and Apply questions ask students to reason about what happens when a part is missing or slow — connecting classroom knowledge of computer hardware to the real device they use at home or at school.

orient.objective: I can name the main parts inside a computer and say what each one does.
orient.courseLink: This is Lesson 2 of Primary 2 Computer Skills. Lesson 1 showed you what computer hardware is — today you build it yourself, and later lessons will show you how software uses these same parts.
successCriteria: I can name the case, motherboard, CPU, RAM and graphics card.
I can say what job each part does inside the computer.
I can explain why a computer needs all its parts working together.
orient.mission: Whoa — this computer arrived in pieces! Put on your builder hat: figure out where each part goes, snap it into place, and power up your very own machine.
steps: Meet the five parts and learn each one's job.
Predict which part you think is the most important.
Build the computer piece by piece in the workshop.
Explain and apply what you have learned.
Answer the Knowledge Check, then generate your Learning Evidence.
orient.realLife: Every laptop, desktop and games console you have ever touched has these exact same five parts hiding inside it — you are about to see what your own computer looks like on the inside.

predict.prompt: Before you build anything: which part do you think a computer could NOT work at all without?
predict.hint: Think about which part actually does the thinking.

investigate.title: The Build Workshop
investigate.lede: Pick a part from the tray, then click the correct spot inside the case. Wrong spot? No problem — just try again. Get all five parts installed to power on your build.

record.intro: Every part you install is logged here automatically.
record.emptyText: No parts installed yet. Head to the workshop and start building.

explain.prompt: Imagine the CPU stopped working, but every other part was fine. Explain what would happen to the computer and why.
explain.lede: Use what you learned about each part's job while building your computer.
expectedPoints: The computer would not be able to think, calculate or run anything at all.
This is because the CPU is the 'brain' — every other part depends on it to process instructions.
Having power, memory and a screen would not matter if nothing can process the instructions.

apply.prompt: A family's home computer takes ages to open programs and games look blocky and slow. Which part would you suggest they upgrade first, and why?
apply.lede: Think about which part's job matches the problem they are having.
expectedPoints: Slow programs opening suggests upgrading the RAM (more working memory) or CPU (faster thinking).
Blocky, slow-looking games point to the graphics card, which is the part that draws what you see on screen.
A good answer names a specific part and links it to the specific symptom described.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Which part is often called the 'brain' of the computer?
knowledgeCheck.explain: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) runs the apps and games and does billions of calculations every second — just like a brain thinking.

options.label: It protects the parts from dust and bumps
It connects every part together so they can talk to each other
It draws the pictures you see on the screen

knowledgeCheck.explain: The motherboard is the 'body' of the computer — it connects the CPU, RAM and every other part so they can work as a team.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Match each part to its job.

pairs.right: Protects everything inside and keeps it cool with fans
Thinks and calculates — the brain of the computer
Draws what you see on the screen

knowledgeCheck.explain: Every part has its own job, and the computer only works well when they all do their job together.

rubric.note: You are graded out of the total marks, shown as a percentage.

criteria.label: Use of evidence
criteria.descriptor: Explain answer uses what was learned while building.

criteria.label: Reasoning
criteria.descriptor: Apply answer links the right part to the right problem.

aiMarkingInstructions: This is a Primary 2 (young primary) student. Mark ONLY the two constructed responses using the rubric and each question's expected_points. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy. Accept simple, age-appropriate wording and do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Report total, percentage, one strength, one correction, one next step, under 60 words, in warm and encouraging language suitable for a young child.
